{"id": "d78c1980-a034-4e69-912f-23960999934b", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "tool_summary", "content": [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "tooluse_nDduvLWaE2h7mecuvolcUq", "status": "success", "content": [{"text": "{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"status\":\"SUCCESS\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails-contextual-grounding-check.html\",\"content\":\"Table of Contents:\\n- Use contextual grounding check to filter hallucinations in responses (char 0-20832)\\n  - Add contextual grounding checks with the console (char 8455-11353)\\n  - Configure contextual grounding checks with the API (char 11354-13848)\\n  - Calling contextual grounding check with Invoke APIs (char 13849-16115)\\n  - Calling contextual grounding check with Converse APIs (char 16116-18201)\\n  - Calling contextual grounding check with ApplyGuardrail API (char 18202-20832)\\n    - How qualifiers affect policy evaluation (char 19396-20832)\\n\\n# Use contextual grounding check to filter hallucinations in responses\\n\\nAmazon Bedrock Guardrails supports contextual grounding checks to detect and filter hallucinations in model\\nresponses when a reference source and a user query is provided. The supported use cases\\ninclude summarization, paraphrasing, and question answering. Standard tier also supports\\nresponses that include reasoning or conversational content. Classic tier does not\\nsupport conversational use cases. For more information, see Safeguard tiers for contextual\\ngrounding checks on this page.\\n\\nContextual grounding checks check for relevance for each chunk processed. If any one\\nchunk is deemed relevant, the whole response is considered relevant as it has the answer\\nto user's query. For streaming API, this can result in scenario where an irrelevant\\nresponse is returned to the user and is only marked as irrelevant after the whole\\nresponse is streamed.\\n\\nContextual grounding checks the following paradigms:\\n\\n* **Grounding** \u2013 This checks if the model\\n  response is factually accurate based on the source and is grounded in the\\n  source. Any new information introduced in the response will be considered\\n  un-grounded.\\n* **Relevance** \u2013 This checks if the model\\n  response is relevant to the user query.\\n\\nConsider an example where the reference source contains \\\"London is the capital of UK.\\nTokyo is the capital of Japan\\\" and the user query is \\\"What is the capital of Japan?\\\". A\\nresponse such as \\\"The capital of Japan is London\\\" will be considered ungrounded and\\nfactually incorrect, where as a response such as \\\"The capital of UK is London\\\" will be\\nconsidered irrelevant, even if it's correct and grounded in the source.\\n\\n**Safeguard tiers for\\ncontextual grounding checks**\\n\\nContextual grounding checks support two safeguard\\ntiers. The tier determines how the check evaluates responses and which\\nlanguages it supports.\\n\\n**Classic tier** evaluates strict grounding. Any\\ninformation in the response that is not stated in the grounding source lowers the\\ngrounding score, including reasonable inferences and conversational phrasing. Classic\\ntier supports English, French, and Spanish.\\n\\n**Standard tier** provides a more robust solution than\\nClassic tier, with support for responses that include reasoning or conversational\\ncontent. Standard tier returns more consistent scores for differently worded responses\\nthat have the same meaning. It supports the same languages as Standard tier content\\nfilters. For more information, see Languages supported by Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. Standard tier requires that your\\nguardrail use cross-Region inference.\\nStandard tier for contextual grounding checks is available in a subset of the\\nAWS Regions that support safeguard tiers. For the list, see Supported Regions for safeguard tiers.\\n\\nIf you don't specify a tier, your guardrail uses Classic tier. The maximum lengths for\\nthe grounding source, query, and response are the same in both tiers.\\n\\n**Note:**\\n\\nWhen a request includes multiple `grounding_source` tags, the guardrail\\ncombines and evaluates all the provided `grounding_source` values\\ntogether, rather than considering each `grounding_source` separately.\\nThis behavior is identical for the `query` tag.\\n\\n**Note:**\\n\\nContextual grounding policy currently supports a maximum of 100,000 characters for\\ngrounding source, 1,000 characters for query, and 5,000 characters for\\nresponse.\\n\\n**Scores and thresholds**\\n\\nContextual grounding checks generate a grounding score and a relevance score for each\\nmodel response, based on the grounding source and user query that you provide. You can\\nconfigure thresholds to filter model responses based on the generated scores. The\\nfiltering threshold determines the minimum score for the model response to be considered\\nas grounded and relevant in your generative AI application. For example, if your\\ngrounding threshold and relevance threshold are each set at 0.7, all model responses\\nwith a grounding or relevance score of less than 0.7 will be detected as hallucinations\\nand blocked in your application. As the filtering threshold is increased, the likelihood\\nof blocking un-grounded and irrelevant content increases, and the probability of seeing\\nhallucinated content in your application decreases. You can configure threshold values\\nof grounding and relevance between 0 and 0.99. A threshold of 1 is invalid as that will\\nblock all content.\\n\\n**Note:**\\n\\nStandard tier and Classic tier evaluate responses differently, so the same\\nresponse can receive different scores in each tier. If you change the tier of an\\nexisting guardrail, test your grounding and relevance thresholds with your own data\\nbefore you deploy the change. For conversational and reasoning use cases on Standard\\ntier, a threshold of 0.7 for grounding and relevance is a reasonable starting\\npoint.\\n\\nContextual grounding checks require 3 components to perform the check: the grounding\\nsource, the query, and the content to guard (or the model response). These are\\nconfigured differently depending on whether you are using Invoke APIs,\\nConverse APIs, or `ApplyGuardrail` directly.\\n\\n* Grounding source \u2013 contextual information needed to answer any user\\n  queries. For example, \\\"London is the capital of UK. Tokyo is the capital of\\n  Japan\\\".\\n* Query \u2013 a question a user may ask. For example, \\\"What is the capital of\\n  Japan?\\\".\\n* Content to guard \u2013 the text that should be guarded relative to the\\n  grounding source and query. For Invoke and Converse APIs, this is\\n  the model response. For example, this can be \\\"The capital of Japan is\\n  Tokyo\\\".\\n\\n**Ungrounded example**\\n\\n* Grounding source - \\\"London is the capital of UK. Tokyo is the capital of\\n  Japan.\\\"\\n* Query - \\\"What is the capital of Japan?\\\"\\n* Content to guard - \\\"The capital of Japan is London.\\\"\\n\\nIn this example, the content to guard is relevant to the query but is ungrounded as it\\ndoes not use the grounding source correctly. This would have a low grounding\\nscore.\\n\\n**Irrelevant example**\\n\\n* Grounding source - \\\"London is the capital of UK. Tokyo is the capital of\\n  Japan.\\\"\\n* Query - \\\"What is the capital of Japan?\\\"\\n* Content to guard - \\\"The capital of UK is London.\\\"\\n\\nIn this example, the content to guard is grounded but not relevant. It uses\\ninformation from the grounding source but does not answer the query. This would have a\\nlow relevance score.\\n\\n**Ungrounded and irrelevant example**\\n\\n* Grounding source - \\\"London is the capital of UK. Tokyo is the capital of\\n  Japan.\\\"\\n* Query - \\\"What is the capital of Japan?\\\"\\n* Content to guard - \\\"It is raining outside.\\\"\\n\\nIn this example, the content to guard is not grounded and not relevant. It neither\\nuses information from the grounding source nor does it answer the query. This would have\\na low grounding and relevance score.\\n\\n**More Examples**\\n\\nConsider a banking application that is designed to answer questions associated with\\nfees and charges.\\n\\nSource:\\n\\n* There are no fees associated with opening a checking account.\\n* The monthly fee for maintaining a checking account is $10.\\n* There is a 1% transaction charge for international transfers.\\n* There are no charges associated with domestic transfers.\\n* The charges associated with late payments of credit card bill is\\n  23.99%.\\n\\nBased on the above source, there can be four scenarios depending on the user's\\nquery.\\n\\n**Grounded and Relevant**\\n\\n* Q: What are the fees associated with checking account?\\n* A: The monthly fee for maintaining a checking account is $10. There are no\\n  charges associated with domestic transfers. However, there is a 1% transaction\\n  charge for international transfers. There are no fees associated with opening a\\n  checking account.\\n\\n**Un-grounded but Relevant**\\n\\n* Q: What is the transaction charge associated with credit card.\\n* A: The transaction charges associated with the credit card is 23.99%.\\n\\n**Grounded but Irrelevant**\\n\\n* Q: What are the charges for using a checking bank account?\\n* A: Based on the information provided, the late payment fee for a credit card\\n  is 23.99%.\\n\\n**Un-grounded and Irrelevant**\\n\\n* Q: What are the charges for using a checking bank account?\\n* A: The charges for the brokerage account are $0.5 per trading\\n  transaction.\\n\\n###### Topics\\n\\n* Add contextual grounding checks with the console\\n* Configure contextual grounding checks with the API\\n* Calling contextual grounding check with Invoke APIs\\n* Calling contextual grounding check with Converse APIs\\n* Calling contextual grounding check with ApplyGuardrail API\\n\\n## Add contextual grounding checks with the console\\n\\n1. Sign in to the AWS Management Console with an IAM identity that has permissions to use the Amazon Bedrock console. Then, open the Amazon Bedrock console at\\n   <https://console.aws.amazon.com/bedrock>.\\n2. From the left navigation pane, choose **Guardrails**, and\\n   then choose **Create guardrail**.\\n3. Without validation, LLMs can produce hallucinations or inaccurate information\\nthat undermines trust. Automated Reasoning checks in Amazon Bedrock Guardrails help solve this problem by using\\nmathematical techniques to validate natural language content against policies you define.\\n\\nUnlike traditional guardrail components that block or filter content based on pattern\\nmatching, Automated Reasoning checks use formal logic to provide structured feedback\\nabout *why* a response is correct or incorrect. This feedback can be\\nused to steer an LLM towards generating content that is provably consistent with your policy.\\nSpecifically, Automated Reasoning checks can:\\n\\n* **Detect factually incorrect statements** in LLM responses by\\n  mathematically proving that generated content contradicts your policy rules.\\n* **Highlight unstated assumptions** where a response is\\n  consistent with your policy but doesn't address all relevant rules, indicating the\\n  response may be incomplete.\\n* **Provide mathematically verifiable explanations** for why\\n  accurate statements are correct, citing the specific policy rules and variable assignments that\\n  support the conclusion.\\n\\nThese capabilities make Automated Reasoning checks different from other Amazon Bedrock Guardrails components.\\nContent filters and topic policies act as binary gates \u2014 they block or allow content.\\nAutomated Reasoning checks act as a verification layer that provides detailed, actionable\\nfeedback you can use to improve responses programmatically.\\n\\n## When to use Automated Reasoning checks\\n\\nAutomated Reasoning checks are most valuable when you need to demonstrate the factual\\nbasis for an LLM's response. Consider using them when your application involves:\\n\\n* **Regulated industries** such as healthcare, human\\n  resources, and financial services, where incorrect information can have legal or\\n  compliance consequences.\\n* **Complex rule sets** such as mortgage approvals, zoning\\n  laws, insurance eligibility, or employee benefits, where multiple conditions interact to\\n  determine an outcome.\\n* **Compliance scenarios** that require auditable AI\\n  responses with mathematically verifiable proof that the response is consistent with your\\n  policies.\\n* **Customer-facing applications** where incorrect\\n  guidance could erode trust, such as chatbots that answer questions about company policies,\\n  product eligibility, or service terms.\\n\\n## What Automated Reasoning checks don't do\\n\\nTo set the right expectations, be aware of the following limitations:\\n\\n* **No prompt injection protection.** Automated Reasoning\\n  checks validate exactly what you send them. If malicious or manipulated content is\\n  provided as input, the validation is performed on that content as-is. To detect and block\\n  prompt injection attacks, use Content filters in combination with Automated Reasoning checks.\\n* **No support for encoded or obfuscated text.** Automated\\n  Reasoning checks evaluate content as plaintext natural language. If *any\\n  part* of the submitted content is encoded or obfuscated \u2014 for example, Base64\\n  (`ZG9ncw==`), hexadecimal escape sequences (`\\\\x63\\\\x61\\\\x74\\\\x73`), or\\n  percent-encoding (`%4d%65%78%69%63%6f`) \u2014 the **entire\\n  submission, including any surrounding plaintext, might not be evaluated**. Make\\n  sure all content you send to Automated Reasoning checks is plaintext.\\n* **No off-topic detection.** Automated Reasoning only\\n  analyzes text that is relevant to the policy. It ignores unrelated content and cannot\\n  tell you whether a response is off-topic. To detect off-topic responses, use topic policies.\\n* **No streaming support.** Automated Reasoning checks\\n  do not support streaming APIs. You must validate complete responses.\\n* **English only.** Automated Reasoning checks currently\\n  support English (US) only.\\n* **Scope limited to your policy.** A `VALID`\\n  result guarantees validity only for the parts of the input captured through policy\\n  variables. Statements that fall outside the scope of your policy's variables are not\\n  validated. For example, \\\"I can submit my homework late because I have a fake doctor's\\n  note\\\" might be deemed valid if the policy has no variable to capture whether the doctor's\\n  note is fake.\\n\\nAutomated Reasoning checks complement other Amazon Bedrock Guardrails features like content filters and topic\\npolicies. For the best protection, use them together. Automated Reasoning extracts formal logic rules\\n   and a schema of variables from your document. A fidelity report is automatically generated\\n   that measures how accurately the extracted policy represents your source documents, with\\n   coverage and accuracy scores and detailed grounding that links each rule and variable back\\n   to the specific statements in your source content. Review the extracted policy and fidelity\\n   report to ensure the policy captures your rules correctly. For more information, see Create your Automated Reasoning policy.\\n2. **Test and refine.** Tests help ensure that your policy\\n   can accurately validate generated content even while you make changes to the policy itself.\\n   Create tests that mimic the questions your users will ask and the responses your LLM might\\n   generate. Automated Reasoning checks use multiple foundation models to translate natural\\n   language into logic representations. Use generated scenarios to validate rule correctness\\n   and QnA tests to validate the natural language to logic translation accuracy. For more information on the permissions\\n   required to enable Automated Reasoning checks, see Permissions for Automated Reasoning policies with ApplyGuardrail.\\n\\n## Availability and language support\\n\\nAutomated Reasoning checks in Amazon Bedrock Guardrails are generally available in the following Regions:\\n\\n* US East (N. Variable descriptions influence the quality of this translation.\\n* **Non-linear arithmetic.** Automated Reasoning checks\\n  might timeout or return TOO_COMPLEX if constraints involve reasoning with non-linear\\n  arithmetic (for example, irrational numbers or exponents).\\n\\n## Pricing\\n\\nAutomated Reasoning checks in Amazon Bedrock Guardrails are charged based on the number of validation requests\\nprocessed. The supported use cases\\\\ninclude summarization, paraphrasing, and question answering. Standard tier also supports\\\\nresponses that include reasoning or conversational content. Classic tier does not\\\\nsupport conversational use cases. For more information, see Safeguard tiers for contextual\\\\ngrounding checks on this page.\\\\n\\\\nContextual grounding checks check for relevance for each chunk processed. If any one\\\\nchunk is deemed relevant, the whole response is considered relevant as it has the answer\\\\nto user\\'s query. For streaming API, this can result in scenario where an irrelevant\\\\nresponse is returned to the user and is only marked as irrelevant after the whole\\\\nresponse is streamed.\\\\n\\\\nContextual grounding checks the following paradigms:\\\\n\\\\n* **Grounding** \u2013 This checks if the model\\\\n  response is factually accurate based on the source and is grounded in the\\\\n  source. The tier determines how the check evaluates responses and which\\\\nlanguages it supports.\\\\n\\\\n**Classic tier** evaluates strict grounding.
